section_name: Section 1: Welcome, Logistics, and Workshop Overview
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 1: Welcome, Logistics, and Workshop Overview

Welcome, everybody. I’m Kristina Smekens, and today we’re working through the Research Report micro workshop. Let’s dive right in.

Informative writing is one of the three major modes of writing. Let’s be clear with our language here. We have the opinion, persuasive, or argumentative mode. We have the informative mode, which some standards call explanatory or expository writing. And then we have narrative writing.

Today, we’re focusing on writing about information. Within that mode, there are many different types or genres. These are the different ways writers convey information.

A writer can summarize, which means pulling together the key information about something. A writer can explain. A writer can compare two different things, such as topics, texts, characters, or even body systems. A writer can write directions or procedural steps.

All of these share the same purpose: to inform the reader. We are writing to teach, explain, describe, and inform.

Our focus today is the research report as a specific genre within informative writing. What makes this genre particularly unique is that it requires a source text. You can write a how-to piece without a source. You can write a compare-contrast about indoor versus outdoor recess without a source. You can summarize an event from yesterday without a source. But research or report writing requires text. It is writing from sources.

That distinction is what we’re going to dive into today.
skill_title: Welcome, Logistics, and Workshop Overview
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 1: Welcome, Logistics, and Workshop Overview

section_name: Section 2: Understanding the Standard
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 2: Understanding the Standard

Let’s draw our attention to the expectations for informative writing and, more specifically, for research and report writing.

When we think about teaching informative writing—whether your standards call it informative, expository, or explanatory—the goal is always the same: informing an audience about a specific concept, complex idea, or topic.

One of the essential facets of research writing is the use of sources. Students are writing with facts, quotes, paraphrases, and citations.

And this is not a standard reserved only for students who are writing in full paragraphs. Even our youngest writers have this expectation. When we think about teaching report writing, we need to get our arms around everything this includes.

The standards often focus heavily on the product—the finished piece. They describe the ingredients that should appear in the final writing. But writing instruction is about building skills within writers.

It is not simply about producing the right piece. It is about building habits, stamina, perseverance, and strategic thinking so students can continue moving forward as writers.
skill_title: Understanding the Standard
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 2: Understanding the Standard

section_name: Section 3: Why Research Writing Feels So Heavy
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 3: Why Research Writing Feels So Heavy

Research or report writing is one of those units that, for many teachers, feels painful.

It is long.
It is complicated.
And often everyone is simply relieved when it is over.

When we stop and list the writer skills involved, it quickly becomes clear why these units take so long.

Students must first choose a topic. That alone can take days.

They may need to narrow the topic and create a focus statement or guiding question.

Then there is the entire process of collecting information from sources:

generating questions 

locating facts 

taking notes 

deciding how many sources are required 

distinguishing between primary and secondary sources 

navigating digital texts 

determining whether a source is credible and relevant 

That is all before they even begin writing.

Then students must read, collect, and take notes.

For primary students, this might mean reading about an animal and lifting facts from a shared text.

For older students, it may involve multiple print and digital sources.

Either way, students must learn how to gather facts from text and then keep track of where those facts came from.

After that comes organization.

This is one of the most overlooked skills in research writing.

Students often know how to collect facts, but they do not know what to do next.

They need explicit instruction in how to organize what they have gathered in preparation for writing.

This is all still prewriting.

None of it is the first draft yet.
skill_title: Why Research Writing Feels So Heavy
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 3: Why Research Writing Feels So Heavy

section_name: Section 4: The First Draft Is Only One Part
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 4: The First Draft Is Only One Part

The informative writing standard often describes what should be visible in the final product:

a beginning 

developed middle ideas 

an ending 

transitions 

precise word choice 

text features 

But all of those visible features rest on a large number of invisible writer skills.

Choosing a topic, collecting facts, organizing ideas, and planning structure are all skills students must possess before they ever write the first sentence.

Only then do we finally get to the draft itself.

At this stage, students need to write:

an introduction 

a focus statement or main idea 

developed body sections 

transitions 

a conclusion 

For younger students, this may be a simple report booklet with pages about body parts, habitat, diet, and predators.

For older students, it may be multiple paragraphs with headings and text features.

But the principle is the same.
skill_title: The First Draft Is Only One Part
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 4: The First Draft Is Only One Part

section_name: Section 5: A Better Approach: Short and Sustained Research
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 5: A Better Approach: Short and Sustained Research

One of the most important ideas in this workshop is this:

Students should not do only one giant research report each year.

The standards specifically call for short as well as sustained research projects.

That means students need more than one opportunity.

If students only do one long report each year, they approach it every time as if it is brand new.

They struggle with note-taking.
They struggle with organization.
They struggle with writing from sources.

The better approach is to do multiple shorter research experiences.

Instead of one enormous unit, consider several shorter report units across the year.

This gives students repeated practice with the core skills.

They become better because they do it more than once.
skill_title: A Better Approach: Short and Sustained Research
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 5: A Better Approach: Short and Sustained Research

section_name: Section 6: The First Research Unit: Teach Only a Few Skills
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 6: The First Research Unit: Teach Only a Few Skills

In the first short report unit, do not teach everything.

Focus on just a few key skills.

For example:

lifting fact phrases from sources 

organizing collected information into categories 

writing a simple topic sentence 

developing body sections 

grouping related facts 

drafting a first version 

That’s it.

Do not spend time on topic choice.
Do not spend time on source evaluation.
Do not spend time on final drafts and heavy revision.

Instead, provide:

the topic 

the source texts 

the structure 

This allows instruction to focus on the writer moves that matter most.
skill_title: The First Research Unit: Teach Only a Few Skills
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 6: The First Research Unit: Teach Only a Few Skills

section_name: Section 7: The Core Problem: Students Freeze at Organization
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 7: The Core Problem: Students Freeze at Organization

One of the biggest problems students face is not gathering information.

It is knowing what to do with it afterward.

They can collect facts.

But then they freeze.

They do not know:

what comes first 

what belongs together 

how to group information 

how to build sections or paragraphs 

This is where explicit instruction matters.

Students need to be taught how to put like ideas together.

This skill transfers across every report topic:

animals 

historical figures 

inventions 

science concepts 

informational reading responses 

The topic changes.
The organizational thinking stays the same.
skill_title: The Core Problem: Students Freeze at Organization
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 7: The Core Problem: Students Freeze at Organization

section_name: Section 8: Teaching Fact Phrases, Note-Taking, and Organization
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 8: Teaching Fact Phrases, Note-Taking, and Organization

If we want students to improve at research writing, we have to stop assuming they already know how to take notes.

Too often, we simply tell students, “Take notes,” and then we’re frustrated when they copy entire sentences, rewrite whole paragraphs from the source, or jot down something so brief that it no longer has meaning.

The problem is not that students are unwilling.

The problem is that note-taking is a skill that must be explicitly taught.

Students need to be shown what a useful fact phrase looks like.

A fact phrase is not a complete sentence copied from the text.

It is also not a single random word with no context.

It is just enough language to preserve the meaning of the fact without rewriting the entire source.

For example, if the text says, Polar bears have thick layers of blubber that help them stay warm in Arctic temperatures, a student should not copy the whole sentence.

Instead, they might jot:

thick blubber keeps body warm

That phrase is short, efficient, and still preserves the meaning.

This is the kind of thinking we must model.

We need to show students how to read a sentence, pause, think about the essential idea, and then condense it into a quick phrase.

That process needs to be modeled over and over again.
skill_title: Teaching Fact Phrases, Note-Taking, and Organization
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 8: Teaching Fact Phrases, Note-Taking, and Organization

section_name: Section 9: Teaching Students What Is Worth Writing Down
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 9: Teaching Students What Is Worth Writing Down

Another key challenge is that students do not always know what information is worth keeping.

When reading from a source, not every detail carries equal weight.

Some details are central to the topic.

Others are supporting examples.

Still others may be interesting but unnecessary.

Students need help learning how to decide what belongs in their notes.

This is where the teacher’s think-aloud becomes critical.

As you read aloud from the source, stop and say things like:

“This sentence tells me where the animal lives. That feels important because habitat is one of the big categories I know I’ll need later.”

Or:

“This detail is interesting, but it’s more of an example than a main fact. I’m going to leave it out for now.”

Students need to hear the invisible decision-making behind note-taking.
skill_title: Teaching Students What Is Worth Writing Down
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 9: Teaching Students What Is Worth Writing Down

section_name: Section 10: Organizing Information Into Categories
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 10: Organizing Information Into Categories

Once students have collected facts, the next step is organization.

This is where many students freeze.

They can gather information, but they do not know how to sort it into meaningful sections.

This is why organization must be taught as its own mini-lesson.

I often tell students that research writing is really about putting like ideas together.

If we are writing about an animal, facts about body parts belong together.

Facts about habitat belong together.

Facts about diet belong together.

Facts about predators belong together.

Those categories then become the structure of the writing.

Each category turns into a paragraph, a page, or a section.

The key is helping students physically sort their facts.

Sometimes this means moving note cards.

Sometimes it means highlighting related details in the same color.

Sometimes it means cutting apart fact strips and regrouping them.

The method can vary.

What matters is that students experience the thinking process of grouping related ideas.
skill_title: Organizing Information Into Categories
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 10: Organizing Information Into Categories

section_name: Section 11: Moving From Notes to Writing
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 11: Moving From Notes to Writing

Once information is grouped, students are much more prepared to draft.

Now they are no longer staring at a random collection of facts.

Instead, they can clearly see the sections of their report.

For example:

Topic: Polar Bears

Body Features 

Habitat 

Diet 

Survival Skills 

Each of these becomes a writing section.

This dramatically reduces overwhelm.

Students no longer feel like they have to write everything all at once.

They simply write one section at a time.

That is an important mindset shift.

We are not asking them to write an entire report.

We are asking them to write about one category of information.

Then the next.

Then the next.

That sequencing helps students build confidence.
skill_title: Moving From Notes to Writing
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 11: Moving From Notes to Writing

section_name: Section 12: Why Repetition Matters
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 12: Why Repetition Matters

This is why I strongly advocate for multiple short research experiences during the year.

Students need repeated practice with:

lifting fact phrases 

determining importance 

grouping information 

drafting from organized notes 

The first time they do this, it will feel slow.

The second time, they improve.

By the third time, the process starts to feel natural.

That is how writer habits are built.

One giant report does not build fluency.

Repeated shorter experiences do.
skill_title: Why Repetition Matters
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 12: Why Repetition Matters

section_name: Section 13: Building the Body Paragraphs and Drafting From Organized Categories
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 13: Building the Body Paragraphs and Drafting From Organized Categories

Once students have collected and organized their facts, the real focus of research writing begins: the body.

This is where I want teachers to put the majority of their instructional energy.

Too often, we spend so much time on the opening that the middle of the report becomes rushed.

But the heart of informative writing is not the introduction.

The heart is the body.

This is where students teach the reader.

This is where they explain the information they gathered from their sources.

This is where the categories they created during prewriting finally become visible in the product.

Each category should now become its own section.

For primary students, that might be a page in a booklet.

For older students, it becomes a paragraph or a full section with a heading.

The structure is the same.

If the report is about an animal, one section might focus on body parts, another on habitat, another on diet, and another on survival behaviors.

If the report is about a historical figure, the sections might include early life, major accomplishments, challenges, and legacy.

The exact topic changes, but the writing move stays the same:

take one organized category and stretch it into developed writing.
skill_title: Building the Body Paragraphs and Drafting From Organized Categories
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 13: Building the Body Paragraphs and Drafting From Organized Categories

section_name: Section 14: Teaching Students to Stay Within One Category
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 14: Teaching Students to Stay Within One Category

One of the biggest challenges in body writing is helping students stay focused.

Students often bounce from one idea to another because all of the facts are sitting in front of them.

This is why the organization work from Part 2 matters so much.

I want students to look only at one group of facts at a time.

I often frame it this way:

“Right now, we are only writing about habitat.”

“Stay in this one lane.”

“Everything in this paragraph must match this category.”

That language helps students understand paragraph unity.

They are not just writing random facts.

They are developing one idea thoroughly before moving on.

This is one of the most important habits in research writing.
skill_title: Teaching Students to Stay Within One Category
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 14: Teaching Students to Stay Within One Category

section_name: Section 15: From Fact Phrases to Full Sentences
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 15: From Fact Phrases to Full Sentences

The next step is teaching students how to stretch fact phrases into full explanatory sentences.

This is where they move from notes to writing.

For example, a student note might say:

thick blubber keeps body warm

That is not yet a sentence for the report.

Now we teach the stretch.

A student might turn that into:

Polar bears have a thick layer of blubber that helps keep their bodies warm in the cold Arctic climate.

This is where the teacher think-aloud is so important.

Students need to hear how we go from shorthand notes to full written language.

I would model this very explicitly:

“I’m looking at my note phrase: thick blubber keeps body warm.”

“Now I’m asking myself, how do I say that in a way that teaches my reader?”

“I want to explain what the blubber does and why it matters.”

This helps students understand that note-taking and drafting are different stages of the process.
skill_title: From Fact Phrases to Full Sentences
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 15: From Fact Phrases to Full Sentences

section_name: Section 16: Teaching Elaboration Within Informative Writing
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 16: Teaching Elaboration Within Informative Writing

Students also need to learn that informative writing is more than listing facts.

A list is not yet a paragraph.

We want explanation.

We want development.

We want students to answer the invisible reader question:

Why does this matter?

For example:

Polar bears have thick blubber.

That is technically a fact.

But it is not yet developed.

A stronger version would be:

Polar bears have thick blubber beneath their skin, which helps insulate their bodies and keep them warm in freezing Arctic temperatures.

Now the reader learns something.

That is the shift from fact listing to informative writing.
skill_title: Teaching Elaboration Within Informative Writing
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 16: Teaching Elaboration Within Informative Writing

section_name: Section 17: Building One Section at a Time
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 17: Building One Section at a Time

I strongly encourage building the body one section at a time.

Do not ask students to draft the entire report in one sitting.

Instead, teach them to complete one category fully.

For example:

Day 1 — habitat
Day 2 — diet
Day 3 — body features
Day 4 — survival behaviors

This pacing helps students stay focused and reduces overwhelm.

It also allows the teacher to model and guide each section.

Students experience repeated practice with the same writing move:

look at organized facts 

convert notes into sentences 

explain the information 

stay within one category 

That repetition builds transfer.
skill_title: Building One Section at a Time
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 17: Building One Section at a Time

section_name: Section 18: Why the Middle Matters Most
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 18: Why the Middle Matters Most

This is the most important idea in this section:

The body is where the teaching happens.

The introduction is important, but it is not the focus.

The body is where students demonstrate their ability to write from sources.

That is why this portion of the workshop places so much emphasis on:

categories 

paragraph unity 

stretching fact phrases 

elaboration 

section-by-section drafting 

This is where research writing instruction truly lives.
skill_title: Why the Middle Matters Most
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 18: Why the Middle Matters Most

section_name: Section 19: Teaching Introductions, Conclusions, and Transitions Without Overemphasizing Them
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 19: Teaching Introductions, Conclusions, and Transitions Without Overemphasizing Them

Once students have strong body sections in place, we can begin teaching the beginning and the ending.

But I want to emphasize something important:

Do not let the introduction become the focus of the unit.

Too often, teachers spend enormous amounts of time teaching elaborate hooks, creative openings, and polished introductions, while the body of the report remains underdeveloped.

In research writing, the introduction has one clear job:

state the topic and prepare the reader for what is coming.

That’s it.

Especially in early report writing experiences, students do not need a long introductory paragraph.

They need a clear topic sentence.

For younger students, this may simply be the title page or the first sentence.

For example:

Polar bears are amazing animals that survive in the Arctic.

That is enough.

It names the topic and sets up the writing.

For older students, this may become a short introductory paragraph, but even then, it should remain concise.

We do not need to overteach this part.

The body is still the priority.
skill_title: Teaching Introductions, Conclusions, and Transitions Without Overemphasizing Them
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 19: Teaching Introductions, Conclusions, and Transitions Without Overemphasizing Them

section_name: Section 20: A Strong Beginning Sentence
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 20: A Strong Beginning Sentence

The skill I want students to master first is writing a single strong beginning sentence.

I want them to say what the writing is about without relying on weak openings such as:

I am writing about polar bears.

or

This report is about Abraham Lincoln.

Instead, I want students to learn how to naturally introduce the topic.

For example:

Abraham Lincoln played a major role in leading the United States during one of its most difficult times.

That is stronger, more informative, and immediately sets the purpose for the reader.

Again, the goal is clarity, not creativity.

This is informative writing.

The purpose is to teach.
skill_title: A Strong Beginning Sentence
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 20: A Strong Beginning Sentence

section_name: Section 21: Teaching Transitions Between Sections
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 21: Teaching Transitions Between Sections

Once students move into multiple sections or paragraphs, transitions become important.

But transitions in informative writing are different from transitions in narrative writing.

We are not moving through time with words like first, next, and then.

Instead, we are helping the reader move from one category of information to another.

This might sound like:

In addition to its physical features…

Another important aspect of the polar bear’s survival is its habitat.

Diet is another key part of understanding this animal.

These transitions help the reader understand that the writing is moving into a new section of information.

I like to teach students that transitions are really road signs for the reader.

They tell the reader where they are headed next.
skill_title: Teaching Transitions Between Sections
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 21: Teaching Transitions Between Sections

section_name: Section 22: Teaching Conclusions
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 22: Teaching Conclusions

Conclusions in research writing also do not need to be overcomplicated.

The conclusion should help the reader feel that the teaching is complete.

For younger students, this may simply be one sentence that wraps up the topic.

For example:

These adaptations help polar bears survive in one of the coldest places on Earth.

For older students, this may become a short concluding paragraph that summarizes the major learning.

Again, the goal is not length.

The goal is clarity.

Students should not simply repeat the introduction.

Instead, they should help the reader leave with the big understanding.
skill_title: Teaching Conclusions
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 22: Teaching Conclusions

section_name: Section 23: Keep the Priority on the Teaching
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 23: Keep the Priority on the Teaching

The biggest idea in this section is that introductions and conclusions support the report, but they are not the core of the work.

The true teaching happens in the body.

If students can:

introduce the topic clearly 

transition smoothly between sections 

conclude with a clear takeaway 

then the report is doing its job.

We do not need to spend disproportionate time polishing openings and endings while the middle remains weak.

Keep the focus where the writing work truly lives.
skill_title: Keep the Priority on the Teaching
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 23: Keep the Priority on the Teaching

section_name: Section 24: Revising and Using Multiple Short Research Units Across the Year
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 24: Revising and Using Multiple Short Research Units Across the Year

One of the most important shifts in this workshop is moving away from the idea that research writing should happen only once a year.

Instead of one long, exhausting report unit, students need multiple short opportunities to write from sources across the year.

This is what builds skill.

No one becomes fluent by doing something once.

Writers improve through repetition.

That means we need several short report experiences that allow students to revisit the same process:

collect facts 

organize information 

draft by category 

introduce the topic 

transition between sections 

conclude clearly 

Each time they do it, they become more efficient and more independent.
skill_title: Revising and Using Multiple Short Research Units Across the Year
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 24: Revising and Using Multiple Short Research Units Across the Year

section_name: Section 25: The First Unit Should Stay Simple
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 25: The First Unit Should Stay Simple

The first research unit of the year should be highly scaffolded.

I would provide:

the topic 

the sources 

the note-taking structure 

the categories 

This keeps the focus on the core writing moves.

Students are learning how research writing works.

They do not need every possible skill introduced at once.

For example, I would not begin with:

source evaluation 

topic choice 

digital searching 

bibliographies 

citations 

formal revision cycles 

Those can come later.

The first unit should focus on writing from sources.
skill_title: The First Unit Should Stay Simple
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 25: The First Unit Should Stay Simple

section_name: Section 26: Add More Independence in the Second Unit
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 26: Add More Independence in the Second Unit

By the second short report unit, we can begin adding another layer of independence.

Now students may:

choose between two or three teacher-provided topics 

gather information from multiple provided texts 

organize their own categories 

draft with less teacher support 

This is where we begin to release more responsibility.

Because students have already practiced the structure once, they are more prepared to handle added complexity.

This second experience is where growth really becomes visible.

Students begin to transfer what they learned in the first unit.
skill_title: Add More Independence in the Second Unit
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 26: Add More Independence in the Second Unit

section_name: Section 27: Build Toward the Larger Research Projectn
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 27: Build Toward the Larger Research Projectn

By the third unit, students are often ready for a more sustained research project.

Now we can begin layering in:

topic narrowing 

source searching 

credibility checks 

paraphrasing from multiple texts 

text features 

citations 

revision and final drafts 

This is the point where a larger research experience makes sense.

Because students have already practiced the foundational moves in shorter cycles, they now have the stamina and strategic thinking needed for a longer project.

The long report should not be the first experience.

It should be the culminating experience.
skill_title: Build Toward the Larger Research Projectn
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 27: Build Toward the Larger Research Projectn

section_name: Section 28: Rethinking Revision
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 28: Rethinking Revision

Another important shift is this:

Not every report needs to go through a full revision and final-draft process.

Sometimes the instructional goal is simply the first draft.

Sometimes the goal is practicing organization.

Sometimes the goal is lifting facts from sources.

Sometimes the goal is paragraph development.

Every short unit does not need to end in a polished product.

This frees teachers to focus on the specific writing skill being taught.

Revision becomes purposeful instead of automatic.
skill_title: Rethinking Revision
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 28: Rethinking Revision

section_name: Section 29: What This Looks Like Across the Year
content:
Teaching the Research Report — Section 29: What This Looks Like Across the Year

A possible yearly flow might look like this:

Unit 1: Short Guided Report

teacher topic 

teacher sources 

note-taking mini-lessons 

category organization 

first draft only 

Unit 2: Short Semi-Guided Report

limited topic choice 

multiple provided sources 

independent organization 

stronger body paragraphs 

Unit 3: Sustained Research Project

student topic 

source selection 

longer drafting 

revision and final product 

This approach aligns beautifully with the standard’s expectation of short as well as sustained research projects.

The Big Takeaway

The biggest takeaway from this section is this:

Research writing should be taught as a repeated process, not a one-time event.

Students need multiple chances to practice the habits of writing from sources.

When we spread the work across the year, the instruction becomes more manageable and the student growth becomes much stronger.

This is how we build confident writers who know what to do with information once they have gathered it.
skill_title: What This Looks Like Across the Year
book_reference: Smekens Teaching the Research Report, Section 29: What This Looks Like Across the Year
